title: UK Regulators Finalise Changes to the High Loan-to-Income Mortgage Limit: The Firm-Level 15% Cap Goes From October 28, 2026, While the 15% Aggregate Limit and the 4.5 Times Income Threshold Stay
summary: On October 14, 2026 the PRA and FCA published final policy on the high loan-to-income mortgage flow limit, removing the firm-level 15% cap on lending at 4.5 times income or more from October 28 while keeping the 15% aggregate limit, measuring firms on a rolling four-quarter basis and the aggregate on a single quarter.
description:
The Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have finalised changes to how the limit on high loan-to-income (LTI) mortgage lending is applied to individual lenders. The final policy was published on October 14, 2026, and the new PRA supervisory statement and FCA guidance take effect on October 28, 2026. This article draws on the FCA's page for its finalised guidance FG26/11 and on a summary of the joint policy statement by the law firm A&O Shearman. The policy statements and the PRA supervisory statement themselves were not reviewed in full, so the rule text should be consulted by any firm applying them.

What the limit is

The Financial Policy Committee (FPC) of the Bank of England recommends a limit on the share of new mortgages that can be lent at high multiples of income. According to the A&O Shearman summary, the FPC defines high LTI as 4.5 times income, and the aggregate flow limit is 15%. In other words, no more than 15% of the total volume of new mortgages in a quarter should be at a multiple of 4.5 times income or more, as a system-wide test.

What was proposed

The FPC made a recommendation in July 2025 that the regulators amend how the flow limit is implemented, giving lenders flexibility while keeping the aggregate flow consistent with the 15% limit. The FCA says the recommendation was that individual lenders should be allowed to increase their share of high LTI lending above 15%. The PRA and the FCA published a joint consultation on April 1, 2026. The FCA's page gives the end of the consultation as July 1, 2026, although its update log also lists a consultation period closing on September 18, a conflict the page does not explain.

What was decided

The regulators are removing the firm-level 15% cap on high-LTI lending. This gives lenders more room to set their own strategies, but the aggregate flow is still tested for consistency with the FPC's 15% limit. The regulators changed the proposal in one respect. Individual firms' high-LTI flows, and any adjustments the regulators require, will be measured on a rolling four-quarter basis, which differs from the consultation proposal. The aggregate flow will be measured on a single calendar quarter, as consulted on.

The regulators received responses on the calibration of the policy, meaning the 4.5 times multiple and the 15% limit, and treated them as outside the consultation's scope. They passed the responses to the FPC for its next review of housing policies. The FPC is to consider them in that review, and nothing in the sources reviewed says it will change them.

Transparency and monitoring

The PRA and FCA will calculate the aggregate high-LTI flow each quarter. The PRA will publish that figure, along with the total volume of in-scope completed mortgages and their share of all completed mortgages. The FCA will publish information when it expects adjustments, and the regulators will publish additional information on mortgage market trends. The FCA will monitor aggregate and individual firm flows as part of its supervisory work, and will monitor compliance with the guidance and any temporary supplemental LTI guidance.

Who is covered

The FCA guidance applies to FCA-authorised mortgage lenders that are not also PRA-authorised or subsidiaries of PRA-authorised firms. The PRA's Rulebook amendments and supervisory statement apply to all firms in scope of the Housing Part of the PRA Rulebook, and the PRA says they also apply at UK subsidiary level for firms not already in scope.

A note on dates

The sources give the key dates consistently: consultation opened April 1, 2026; final policy and guidance issued October 14, 2026; new documents effective October 28, 2026. The one inconsistency is the FCA page's two references to when the consultation closed, July 1 in the main text and September 18 in the update log. Because the consultation outcome was published on October 14, the exact closing date does not affect the current rules, but readers citing the consultation should check the original paper.

Documents and dates

The joint policy statement is published as PRA PS19/26 and FCA PS26/20. The PRA's new supervisory statement is SS2/26, which sets out governance and risk management expectations. The FCA's non-Handbook guidance FG26/11 replaces its earlier general guidance FG14/8 of October 2014, as revised by FG17/2 in February 2017 and FG25/4 in July 2025. Both new documents take effect on October 28, 2026.

What it means for borrowers

The sources reviewed do not say that lenders will approve more high-LTI loans, and any such effect would depend on lenders' choices. Borrowers should expect that availability of mortgages at high multiples of income may vary by lender. What the sources do not say includes the expected effect on house prices, the number of additional loans, or whether lenders have already announced changes, and this article makes no claim about them.
source_name: Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority (policy statements PS19/26 and PS26/20 and guidance FG26/11, October 14, 2026)

key_points: The PRA and FCA issued their final policy on October 14, 2026 as PRA PS19/26 and FCA PS26/20, following a consultation that opened on April 1, 2026 and, according to the FCA, closed on July 1.

The main change removes the firm-level 15% cap on high loan-to-income mortgage lending, giving lenders more room to set their own high-LTI strategies, while the aggregate flow is still expected to stay consistent with the Financial Policy Committee's 15% limit.

High loan-to-income is defined as 4.5 times income or more; the regulators treated responses on the 4.5 times and 15% calibrations as outside the consultation and passed them to the FPC for its next housing review.

Firms' high-LTI flows will be measured on a rolling four-quarter basis, which changed from the consultation proposal of fixed quarters, while the aggregate flow is measured on a single calendar quarter.
PRA supervisory statement SS2/26 and FCA guidance FG26/11 take effect on October 28, 2026, and the PRA will publish the aggregate high-LTI flow each quarter.
why_it_matters: The limit affects how many mortgages lenders can offer at high multiples of income, which matters to first-time buyers and to anyone trying to borrow more relative to earnings. The change gives individual lenders flexibility while the regulators keep a system-wide cap, so access may vary more between lenders.

title: APRA Finalises Reinsurance Rule Changes Letting Australian Insurers Use Catastrophe Bonds Without a Reinstatement, Cutting Approval Requirements From January 2027
summary: On July 7, 2026 the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority finalised amendments to its general insurance reinsurance framework: a reinstatement is not required where one is typically unavailable, as with catastrophe bonds; the Appointed Actuary can decide capital treatment for many arrangements; and the new rules take effect on January 1, 2027.
description:
On July 7, 2026, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) published a response paper finalising amendments to the framework that governs how general insurers use reinsurance. The headline change is that insurers are being given easier access to alternative reinsurance, a category that includes catastrophe bonds and other insurance-linked securities, which transfer risk to capital-market investors rather than to a traditional reinsurer. The final prudential standards, guidance and reporting standards take effect on January 1, 2027. This article draws on APRA's response paper, with a law-firm summary of the same package from Regulation Tomorrow, and it separates what the regulator has finalised from what it has not.

How the package came about

APRA first sought feedback on the direction of the review in November 2024. In October 2025 it consulted on draft prudential standards, guidance and reporting standards and received seven submissions. According to the response paper, respondents broadly supported the proposals and asked for some clarifications, which APRA has partly addressed. Regulation Tomorrow's summary says APRA proceeded with the proposals as consulted on, with minor clarifications. The instruments affected include the prudential standards GPS 115 (Insurance Risk Charge), GPS 116 (Insurance Concentration Risk Charge), GPS 230 (Reinsurance Management) and CPS 320 (Actuarial and Related Matters), the practice guides GPG 116 and GPG 245, and a set of reporting standards.

The reinstatement change

A reinstatement is a feature of traditional catastrophe reinsurance under which cover that is used up by a loss is restored, usually for an additional premium, so that the insurer is protected against a second event in the same period. Catastrophe bonds usually do not offer this: once a bond pays out, the protection is used up.

The final rules say a reinstatement is not required for arrangements where one is typically unavailable. APRA's guidance states that "catastrophe bonds are generally considered arrangements where a reinstatement is not typically available." In place of the requirement, insurers must decide how they would manage the risk of not having a reinstatement, including how cover would be restored where relevant, and record the approach in their Reinsurance Management Strategy, or ReMS. For APRA's Natural Perils Horizontal Requirement, reinstatement costs must be included if the insurer assumes cover will be reinstated. They are not required in the Natural Perils Vertical Requirement for arrangements that have no typical reinstatement.

Capital and the 1-in-200 standard

APRA says it judged the risk of a material shift in market behaviour to be low and did not add a capital charge for alternative reinsurance. For reinsurance that does not cover all perils and regions, such as single-peril cover, APRA makes a net whole-of-portfolio approach mandatory. APRA says this preserves the existing level of protection against a 1-in-200-year all-perils event. In other words, the regulator is making it easier to use alternative products while insisting that an insurer's overall protection is judged across its whole portfolio, not product by product.

Less need for APRA approval

A second theme is efficiency. For many arrangements, the Appointed Actuary (AA) will determine the capital treatment by default. The response paper gives examples: adverse development cover, which protects against claims on past business turning out worse than expected, top-and-drop cover, and single-peril catastrophe bonds with an indemnity trigger. APRA approval is still needed for complex, material arrangements, including those with parametric triggers, which pay on a measured event such as wind speed rather than on the insurer's actual losses, industry loss warranties and certain stop-loss covers. APRA will not set a numerical materiality threshold; insurers and appointed actuaries may refer to guidance from the Actuaries Institute. Simple arrangements such as traditional quota share and catastrophe excess-of-loss cover need no AA or APRA involvement.

Other changes to GPS 230 and related standards

Several smaller changes are worth noting. Disputes under reinsurance contracts must be arbitrated in Australia, and reinsurance payments must be made in Australia. The requirement that contracts be signed and stamped is replaced by a requirement that they be legally binding between all parties. Material catastrophe modelling information must be included in the Reinsurance Arrangement Statement (ReAS), with supporting detail held separately for APRA on request, and insurers do not need to resubmit their ReAS solely because of the changes; changes should appear in the next scheduled submission. GPS 116 now clarifies that allowances for non-modelled risk should capture demand surge, underinsurance and policy features that increase loss.

What was not adopted

One suggestion was not taken up now. An eight-week collateral grace period had been suggested. APRA did not adopt it in this package and says it will consult on the idea through its 2026 minor prudential framework updates, so it remains open.

Timing and reporting

The new framework applies from January 1, 2027. Updated reporting forms are planned for the APRA Connect Test environment in September 2026, with taxonomy artefacts released before then.

What it means

For insurers, the changes lower regulatory friction for catastrophe bonds and similar structures, and reduce the number of arrangements that need APRA approval, but they add documentation: an insurer using a bond without a reinstatement must show it has thought about the gap. For policyholders, the stated objective is to give insurers flexibility while keeping appropriate safeguards. Whether the changes will lower reinsurance costs, or lead to more Australian cat bond issuance, is not something the response paper claims, and this article does not predict. The effect will depend on market conditions and on how insurers and investors respond after 2027. Readers who need the precise wording should consult the final instruments on APRA's website. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (response paper, finalising amendments to the general insurance reinsurance framework), with Regulation Tomorrow

key_points: APRA published its response paper on July 7, 2026, after consultations in November 2024 and October 2025 (the latter drew seven submissions), and the final standards, guidance and reporting standards take effect on January 1, 2027.

A reinstatement is not required where one is typically unavailable, and APRA's guidance says catastrophe bonds are generally such arrangements; insurers must decide how they would manage the risk of having no reinstatement and record it in their Reinsurance Management Strategy.

The Appointed Actuary will set capital treatment by default for many arrangements, such as adverse development cover, top-and-drop cover and single-peril catastrophe bonds with an indemnity trigger, while APRA approval remains for complex material deals such as parametric triggers and industry loss warranties.

APRA judged the risk of a material shift in market behaviour to be low and added no capital charge for alternative reinsurance; for single-peril cover it requires a net whole-of-portfolio approach to keep the 1-in-200-year all-perils protection level.
APRA did not adopt a suggested eight-week collateral grace period now, and will consult on it through its 2026 minor prudential framework updates.
why_it_matters: Australian insurers face rising catastrophe losses and pay a lot for traditional reinsurance. By removing a rule that made catastrophe bonds and similar products hard to fit into the prudential framework, APRA widens the tools insurers can use, while keeping safeguards for policyholders. How much insurers actually use those tools will only become clear after the rules start in 2027.
